result:
Lichen is not one thing. It is a partnership: a fungus that builds the house and an alga or bacterium that makes the food. Neither can live on bare rock alone, but together they settle places nothing else will take—tombstones, lava fields, the windward side of Antarctic boulders.

What I like most about lichen is its pace. Some species grow less than a millimeter a year. A patch the size of a dinner plate on a mountain rock may have been there when the Romans were building roads. Geologists use this, in fact; they measure lichen to estimate how long ago a glacier retreated and left a stone exposed. The method is called lichenometry, which is a word I'm glad exists.

There is something reassuring about an organism that does so little so persistently. Lichen doesn't chase anything. It sits in the sun, drinks fog, and over centuries breaks rock into the first thin layer of soil. Everything that grows on a mountainside later—the moss, the grass, the pines—owes something to that patient crust.

We tend to admire speed: the cheetah, the falcon, the startup. But most of the world was built slowly, by things barely noticed while they worked. Lichen has survived exposure to open space and can dry out for years, then revive with a little water. Its whole strategy is staying put.

Next time you pass an old stone wall, look at the gray-green and orange patches. They aren't stains. They're tenants, and they're in no hurry.
